1. Platform identity summary

Charlie's professional presence is currently fragmented across three platforms serving different economic and relational purposes:

Platform Listed offering Platform role Artist revenue model
Fiverr Rap verse — $350/verse Marketplace — buyer-fee model ~80% of listed price after fees
AirGigs UK rap vocals — $200 Marketplace — different fee structure Fee terms not publicly verified
Bandcamp Artist-owned presence Direct-to-fan, no middleman ~82–85% on digital, 90%+ on merch

The current model has Charlie receiving platform-mediated commissions where marketplaces define his value ceiling and extract significant margin. The opportunity is to reframe Bandcamp not as a passive presence but as the anchor of an artist-controlled commercial identity.

2. Bandcamp Friday — what it is and how Charlie should be using it

Bandcamp Friday is a recurring promotional event (typically the first Friday of each month) where Bandcamp waives its revenue share entirely, passing 100% of sales directly to the artist.

Current likely use: Passive — profile exists, releases may be posted, no active promotion cycle.

What active use looks like:

Release cadence

  • Time instrumental releases, remix packs, and verse-only versions to land on Bandcamp Friday.
  • A $5–$15 downloadable instrumental or a limited-edition verse stem pack released on Bandcamp Friday earns full margin with zero platform cut.
  • Stack Bandcamp Friday drops with social pushes (TikTok, IG Reels, Bluesky) the Tuesday–Thursday prior so the algorithm has runway before the drop.

Pricing architecture

Product type Suggested price Why
Single instrumental $5–$10 name-your-price Low friction, builds catalogue buyers
Verse stem pack (3 takes) $15–$25 Producers pay for options — this is a real market
Full EP (5 tracks) $7–$12 Competitive with streaming, full margin
Limited collab bundle $20–$50 Scarcity + co-signed releases drive collector behavior

Fan relationship

Bandcamp is the only major platform where buyers follow artists, not algorithms. Every Bandcamp Friday sale is also a list-building event. Charlie should treat each drop as a newsletter capture moment, not just a revenue event.

What this changes for the 50-ways-to-leave-another offer

A Charlie J who runs structured Bandcamp Friday drops is not just a freelance rapper — he is an independent music business with a direct-to-fan revenue channel. That shifts the offer from "pay per verse" toward "co-release with shared Bandcamp presence," which is materially more valuable to both parties.

3. Sync licensing — current potential and gap analysis

What sync licensing is

Synchronization (sync) licensing is the right to pair a composition and/or master recording with moving image — trailers, games, ads, TV, film, branded content. It is one of the most durable and high-margin revenue streams available to independent artists because:

  • It pays upfront (sync fee) plus backend (performance royalties via PRO).
  • It does not require streaming volume.
  • It rewards distinctive voice and clear ownership documentation.

Charlie's current sync potential

Strengths: - UK rap vocal — a specific, identifiable sonic identity that sync supervisors can place. Generic vocals do not get placed; accents and character do. - Multi-platform presence proves he is an active working artist, not a ghost profile — supervisors verify this. - $200–$350 price point for session work demonstrates he can operate at indie-budget rates, which is the exact budget tier for most independent film, YouTube premium, and branded content work.

Gaps: - No evidence of a public-facing sync-ready catalogue — stems, metadata, PRO registration, and ISRC codes are necessary before any supervisor can clear a track. - No documented split sheet history. Sync supervisors will not place a track where ownership is ambiguous. Every verse Charlie records needs a co-writer agreement on file before it is pitched. - No sync-specific metadata tagging. Bandcamp, AudioSalad, and DistroKid all support genre, mood, tempo, and instrumentation tags. These are the fields supervisors search. - No demonstrated experience with brief-driven composition — sync work means writing to picture or to a creative brief, not free-form session delivery.

What Charlie needs to do to grow this skill

Stage 1 — Documentation (immediate, no cost) 1. Register with a PRO (PRS for Music as a UK artist) if not already done. 2. Assign ISRCs to every released track via DistroKid, Amuse, or direct registration. 3. Create a split sheet for every past and future collaboration. Use a template like the one in templates/split-sheet.md in this repository. 4. Export stems for every completed track. Archive them in a controlled Drive folder with clear version history.

Stage 2 — Catalogue preparation (30–90 days) 1. Re-tag all Bandcamp releases with sync-relevant metadata: BPM, key, mood descriptors (e.g., "gritty," "urgent," "melancholic"), instrumentation, and vocal type. 2. Create 30-second and 60-second edits of existing tracks — standard brief lengths for ad and trailer placements. 3. Upload an instrumental version of every vocal track. Many sync placements use instrumental only, or swap between vocal and instrumental versions in post.

Stage 3 — Pitching infrastructure (60–120 days) 1. Build a one-page sync EPK: voice profile, genre, mood range, sample placements (even self-produced mockups), PRO affiliation, and split/clearance contact. 2. Submit to non-exclusive sync libraries: Musicbed, Artlist, Pond5, Soundsnap — these pay non-exclusive licensing fees and build placement history. 3. Target brief-driven platforms: Taxi, Matchmaker.fm, and Music Gateway all issue regular briefs from TV/film/ad buyers. Responding to briefs is the fastest way to build a sync track record.

Stage 4 — Rate structure Once placement history exists, indie sync fees for a UK rap vocal in branded content typically range from $250–$2,500 per placement at the budget tier. TV and film run higher. The ceiling is not the skill gap — the documentation and discoverability gaps are.

4. Charlie as sync agent for the IBLoud IVXX Story Lab

What the Story Lab needs

The ibloud-ivxx-story-lab repository documents a transmedia narrative project (IBLoud IVXX) built around an original character, a distributed story arc across platforms, and a soundtrack map that currently has significant clearance gaps. From the Story Lab's README:

"A rights-aware catalogue incubator for replacing uncleared mashups with original compositions."

Tracks currently listed as "reference only" or "research reference pending provenance review" need to be replaced with original, fully cleared compositions before the project can move to commercial or licensed use. The Story Lab's CLEARANCE-LEDGER.md and TRACKLIST.md both document this gap explicitly.

What Charlie brings to that gap

Charlie's vocal profile — UK rap, distinctive accent, session-proven delivery — maps directly to the Story Lab's narrative tone: urban, character-driven, textured. He is not a generic session vocalist. His voice carries the "signal, witness, archive" quality that IBLoud IVXX is built around.

Specifically: - "iCall" (initiating signal) and "Nasty Game" (celebrity spectacle as conflict) are both narrative-function tracks where a distinctive vocal presence drives the story, not background texture. - His AirGigs presence at $200/UK rap vocal positions him at exactly the budget tier the Story Lab can absorb for proof-of-concept replacements without requiring a full production budget.

Sync agent framing — what this means practically

A sync agent relationship between Charlie and the Story Lab would work as follows:

Role Charlie J Loptr Lab / IBLoud IVXX Story Lab
Creates Original vocal performances to replace uncleared tracks Story arc, character, brief, and placement context
Owns His master and composition share The project framework, narrative IP, and sync pitch
Earns Session fee (upfront) + sync royalty share (backend) Licensing revenue from Story Lab placements
Documents Split sheet, ISRC, PRO registration CLEARANCE-LEDGER.md entries, rights envelope
Controls Withdrawal/consent at any stage Cannot place or represent his work without consent

This is not a work-for-hire arrangement. Charlie retains his composition share. Loptr Lab functions as the sync agent: identifying placement opportunities, handling pitch infrastructure, and splitting backend royalties according to the agreed split sheet.

Immediate next steps if Charlie agrees

  1. Agree on one track from the Story Lab TRACKLIST.md to replace with an original co-written and co-performed composition.
  2. Execute a rights envelope (template in templates/rights-envelope.md) for that track before any recording begins.
  3. Charlie registers the composition with PRS and assigns an ISRC.
  4. Loptr Lab adds the track to CLEARANCE-LEDGER.md as CLEARED — original composition, co-authored [Charlie J / Dominique Devereaux], split sheet on file.
  5. The track is released on Bandcamp (including on a Bandcamp Friday) with sync metadata tags, making it simultaneously a direct-to-fan release and a sync-ready asset.

That single track serves as proof of concept for the full catalogue replacement strategy and demonstrates Charlie's sync viability with a documented, published placement.
